sentences.text: Brief facts of the case are as under: The plaintiff filed this suit against the defendant seeking partition and separate possession of half share in the suit schedule property, including immovable and movable assets, gold, vehicles, profits from the agarbathi business, mesne profits, and permanent injunction against dispossession.
The plaintiff and the defendant are children of the late M.Srinivasalu and Smt.Umadevi.
The mother died on 20.11.2010 and the father on 03.11.2019.

The father had purchased and constructed a three-storied house at No.94/5, Vasavi Pooja Layout,
Basavanagudi, Bengaluru, (plaint schedule and the item No.1 of the written schedule property)
where both siblings resided.
He also ran an agarbathi business, owned vehicles, gold, and maintained bank accounts.
No partition was made during the parents' lifetime, and the properties are claimed to be Hindu Undivided Family assets.

After the parents' deaths, the plaintiff resides on the first floor, while the defendant allegedly took possession of the shop, remaining portions, and profits, refusing partition despite repeated requests.

The defendant, in her counterclaim, contends that the properties, including another property at 185, Kumbarpet Main Road, Bengaluru, (Item Nos.2 & 3 of the written statement schedule property) were self-acquired by the parents, admits both parties are Class I heirs, and seeks partition, separate possession, and accounting of rents,
movables, gold, vehicles, and bank balances after adjustment of debts incurred by the parents.

The plaintiff denies the counterclaim, asserting that No.94/5 is ancestral with the plaintiff entitled to half share, property at 185 is her self-acquired property, and that the defendant is unlawfully retaining rents, vehicles, gold, and bank balances.

The properties in dispute include House No.94/5,
Vasavi Pooja Layout, property at 185, Kumbarpet Main Road including shop and undivided land share, two vehicles, gold and silver, and bank balances.
10.

The core issue which needs to be determined in the present suit is as to whether the suit schedule properties and movables are joint Hindu Undivided Family assets requiring partition between the plaintiff and defendant, or whether certain properties, including property at 185,
Kumbarpet Main Road, are self-acquired by the plaintiff or father, and to what extent the parties are entitled to partition, separate possession, and share of income, profits, and assets.

11. Upon a careful perusal of the pleadings and consideration of the oral and documentary evidence on record, the issues are answered as follows:
Issue Nos.1 & 2: These issues are closely related to each other and therefore are taken up together for joint discussion at a stretch in order to avoid repetitive discussion of facts.

The plaintiff approached this Court seeking partition and separate possession of the plaint schedule property, being House No. 94/5, Vasavi Pooja Layout, Basavanagudi,
Bengaluru, (also Item No.1 of the written statement schedule property) along with movable assets, vehicles, and a share in the profits of the business carried on by the deceased father.

The property purchased by late Srinivasulu and Smt.Umadevi is their self-acquired property, and upon their intestate death, it devolves upon the plaintiff and defendant as Class I heirs under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
Such property does not automatically become coparcenary or Hindu Undivided Family property unless there is evidence of blending or ancestral origin.

The plaintiff's case Preethi R vs Shruthi P R on 4 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/151747694/
8 was that the property was acquired by her parents, Smt.Umadevi and M.Srinivasalu,
and remained joint family property, never partitioned during their lifetime.

sentences.text: The plaint and accompanying documents, marked at Exs.P.1 to P.15, reveal that the plaint property was originally purchased by the mother as per Ex.P.5 and later stood in the father's name as per documents marked at Exs.P.1, P.2, P.6, P.7.
Encumbrance certificates marked at Exs.P.11 & 12 further demonstrate that there were no transfers or alienations inconsistent with joint family ownership.

The plaintiff examined herself as PW-1, along with supporting witnesses, that she and the defendant lived together with their parents, enjoyed the property jointly, and that no formal partition had ever taken place.
She also relied on documentary evidence to substantiate claims over the vehicles, movable assets, and rents collected from parts of the property.

12. The defendant, while admitting that both she and the plaintiff are legal heirs, contended that the property was self-acquired by the parents, and claimed entitlement to partition only after adjusting outstanding debts and expenses.

She produced letters and handwritten settlements marked at Exs.D.3, D.4, D.6, D.10 indicating the father's wish to divide his properties among his daughters, as well as a memorandum of understanding regarding loans marked at Ex.D.7.
The defendant also relied on a legal notice marked at Ex.D.1 and postal acknowledgment marked at Ex.D.2 to assert her claim to partition, including her share in vehicles, gold, and bank balances.
13. On careful scrutiny of the evidence, it is apparent that the documents produced by the defendant,
while reflecting the father's intentions, do not constitute legally binding instruments of partition.
There is no evidence of division by metes and bounds, nor any conveyance transferring exclusive rights to either daughter.

The plaintiff's evidence, supported by the khatha records, BBMP endorsements, tax receipts, sale deeds, and encumbrance certificates, establishes continuous joint possession and enjoyment by both daughters with their parents, confirming the joint character of the property.
The settled legal position is that mere possession or use by a coparcener does not convert joint property into self-acquired property, and partition requires clear evidence of division.
The self- acquisition must be clearly established or in the absence of such proof, property held in family without partition continues to be joint property.

14. Considering the pleadings, oral testimony, and documentary evidence (Exs.P.1-P.15 and Exs.D.1-D.10), it is concluded that the plaint schedule property/Item No. 1 of the written statement,
is a joint Hindu Undivided Family property.
The plaintiff is entitled to one-half share in the property and related movable assets.
The defendant's contentions regarding self-acquisition and exclusive entitlement are unsubstantiated.
The claim for partition and separate possession by the plaintiff is therefore upheld, subject to adjustment of legally proven debts.
Accordingly, this Court answers the Issue Nos.1 & 2 in Affirmative.

sentences.text: The present dispute revolves around the ownership and division of item Nos.2 to 5 of the plaint schedule property.

The plaintiff claims that item No.2 was purchased by her father, late M.Srinivasulu, in her name out of love and affection when she was a minor, arguing that this property should be treated as her self-acquired property and the defendant has no right over the same.
Conversely, the defendant contends that all these properties, including item No.2, are joint family assets, and she is entitled to an equal share in their partition.

16. The plaintiff relies on documentary evidence showing registration in her name, namely Ex.P.8 &
Ex.P.8(a) (sale deed for item No.2), Ex.P.9 (BBMP endorsement), and Ex.P.10 (tax receipt),
asserting that ownership in her name establishes exclusive rights.

The defendant, however,
produced a series of documents demonstrating the father's clear intention to divide his properties among both daughters: Ex.D.1 (legal notice seeking partition), Ex.D.3 (letter of late Srinivasulu stating his wish to divide the properties), and Exs.D.4 & D.10 (handwritten settlement letters concerning property, loans, and rents).

Oral evidence also corroborates that both daughters contributed to family responsibilities and upkeep, underscoring the father's intention to treat the properties as family assets rather than gifts to one child alone.

17. That, while the plaintiff emphasizes that item No.2 stands in her name, Indian jurisprudence has consistently held that beneficial ownership depends on the intention of the person providing the funds, not merely on the registered name.

The counsel for the plaintiff relies upon the judgment passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Meenakshi Ammal v. S.Vijayalekshmi & Ors reported in 2017 0 Supreme (Ker) 402, wherein it is held that property purchased in the name of a wife or daughter can still be treated as a family asset if the purchaser's intention was for family benefit.

sentences.text: The Court noted that the statutory presumption under Section 3(2) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, favoring the ostensible titleholder, can be rebutted by evidence demonstrating the true intent of the transferor.

18. In Valliammal v. Subramanian reported in AIR 2004 SC 4187, the Hon'ble Apex Court emphasized that the source of purchase money and the purpose behind registering property in another's name are critical in determining whether the transaction was benami or intended for the family.

The plaintiff, being a minor at the time of purchase, could not have independently acquired property.

sentences.text: That as per Section 3(2) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, a property purchased in the name of a daughter is presumed to be for her benefit.
However, this presumption is rebuttable.
In the present case, the presumption stands rebutted as the plaintiff herself admitted the signature of her father on Ex.D.3 & 4 and thereby her father's intention to divide he properties.
Further, the financial contribution, absence of independent income of the plaintiff at the time of purchase and conduct of the parties treating it as common asset.
20. In the Indian social context, family property is commonly treated as a shared resource, reflecting the collective contributions and responsibilities of all children.
Fathers frequently register property in the name of one child, often a minor, without intending to confer exclusive ownership.

The admission of the father's signatures on Exs.D.3 and D.4 confirms that the father's intention was to create a family estate to be equitably shared, consistent with societal norms valuing fairness among siblings.
21. Therefore, in the light of above findings and observations this Court holds that item Nos.2 to 5 are joint family properties of plaintiff and defendant.
The defendant is therefore entitled to an equal share, and the plaintiff's claim that item No.2 is self-acquired is rejected.
Accordingly, this Court answers the Issue No.3 in the Affirmative and Issue No.4 in the Negative.
22. Issue No.5:
The plaintiff contended that the defendant had not paid the proper court fee in respect of her counterclaim.
Upon examination of the records and the pleadings, it is apparent that no credible evidence was led to substantiate this contention.
The defendant's counterclaim was filed in accordance with procedural requirements, and the documents do not reveal any deficiency in court fee payment.
In view of this, the contention of the plaintiff fails.
Accordingly, this Court holds that the counter claim of the defendant is maintainable and answers this Issue in the Negative.
23. Issue Nos.6 & 7: These issues are interconnected with each other and therefore are taken up together for joint discussion.
